title: One word of peace (100–102)
hook: better than a thousand empty words is one word that brings peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, calm thought: when the mind is quiet, word and deed follow. Your line: calm thought, calm word. Today, chapter eight: the thousands.

How many words went through your day yesterday? Emails, texts, meetings, podcasts, a thread of three hundred comments, a group chat that never stops. Tens of thousands, easily. Now try to remember one that actually helped: that settled you, or showed you something true, or made you kinder. Maybe you can find one. Maybe you can't. The eighth chapter of the Dhammapada is built on that arithmetic: thousands against one.
screen: `TENS OF THOUSANDS OF WORDS.` → `WHICH ONE HELPED?` → `THOUSANDS AGAINST ONE.`

segments.voice: Verse one hundred, in Müller's English: “Even though a speech be a thousand (of words), but made up of senseless words, one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet.” The test of a word isn't how impressive it is, or how many came with it. It's whether the person who hears it becomes quiet: settled, at peace. Verses one hundred one and one hundred two say it twice more: a thousand verses of empty words, or a hundred, can't match one verse that brings peace. The commentary ties verse one hundred one to a striking story. A man named Bahiya survived a shipwreck, came ashore wearing nothing but bark, and people began to treat him as a holy man. Troubled, he set out to find the Buddha, and found him on his alms round in the street. Bahiya begged to be taught right there. Twice the Buddha said it wasn't the time. The third time, he gave him a teaching of just a few lines, roughly: in the seen, let there be only the seen; in the heard, only the heard. No extra story laid on top. Bahiya understood, the story says, on the spot. A handful of words was all he needed. The chapter isn't against talking, or reading, or long teachings; you and i are reading a whole book together. But among all the words, look for the one that calms. And when you're the one speaking, try to be that word.
screen: `A THOUSAND SENSELESS WORDS.` · `THE TEST: DOES IT BRING QUIET?` · `BAHIYA, IN THE STREET.` · `IN THE SEEN, ONLY THE SEEN.` · then, large: `ONE WORD THAT CALMS.`

segments.voice: Let the noise of the day's words drift away, and try Bahiya's teaching: as you hear a sound, let it be only the sound, with no name for it and no story about it; as you feel the breath, only the feeling. Then think of one person you'll talk to today, and let one simple sentence form that's true and useful, and might leave them a little calmer.
Sahassa. A thousand: better than a thousand empty words is a single word that, when someone hears it, brings them quiet.
Your line: one word that calms. In the seen, only the seen. That's day one hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often stress brief, well-chosen teaching, and the story of Bahiya, awakened by a teaching of a few lines, is widely told as an example.

original.note: Pali: a thousand, the title of chapter eight (Sahassa Vagga).

trapdoor: what you thought: 'one word is better than a thousand' is a pitch for short speeches.
what it means: the worth of words is whether they bring peace to the one who hears them.
what a scholar hears: the Bahiya teaching ('dittha ditthamattam bhavissati,' in the seen will be merely the seen) is in the Udana (1.10); the commentary ties it to verse 101.
